hints.hint: In two-speaker "I don't know" puzzles, first name the feature that is unknown to the speakers. If the public number's role (sum vs product) is unknown, a speaker holding v has at most two candidate partners: public minus v, and public divided by v when it divides exactly. Keep only candidates obeying the domain rules (natural number), then count: exactly one means "I know", two or more means "I don't know". Never collapse to one reading mid-solution; a candidate dies only from a domain rule or an announcement. The decisive step most attempts skip: convert the first announcement into the set A of values that speaker could be holding, then when testing the second speaker keep a candidate partner only if it lies in A, and recount inside A. That cross-filter, not raw ambiguity, is what pins the answer. If nothing survives, recheck A instead of reporting an unjustified divisor.
hints.subagent_summary: My 8 public rollouts scored 2/8 (execution 149.97); all six failures enumerated the divisor pairs of the public number but never fed Sasha's announcement back as a constraint on Masha's candidate partners, so they collapsed to a single reading, declared "the partner is uniquely determined, contradiction", and emitted an unjustified divisor (143 three times, 11 once) while two burned the token cap looping on that contradiction. The revision keeps the two-candidates-per-private-value counting rule but adds the missing mechanism explicitly: turn the earlier announcement into a set of admissible partner values and re-count each later speaker's candidates only within that set.

hints.hint: For (z-a)^n = c(z-b)^n, b possibly 0, never enumerate the n roots. Take moduli in two separate steps: first |z-a|^n = |c||z-b|^n, then nth-root that: |z-a| = k|z-b| with k = |c|^(1/n). The 1/n applies to |c| alone, never to an equation still holding nth powers. k = 1 means a line, the bisector of a and b. Else a known Apollonius circle: z-a = k(z-b) and z-a = -k(z-b) end a diameter, so center = (a - k^2 b)/(1 - k^2) and radius = k|a-b|/|1 - k^2|. Use that; skip sampling roots. The center is off it. Report what is asked.
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 round-5 rollouts scored 1, so training is saturated and the loss is transfer plus wasted tokens. The dominant failure was the incumbent's compressed modulus line: rollouts wrote |z-a|^n = |c|^(1/n)|z-b|^n (mixing the power and the root in one step) and then carried a wrong ratio for thousands of tokens before self-correcting, with the two longest rollouts (12.2k and 7.0k tokens, 37 and 35 hedges) spending most of their length on that constant. A second sink is that the incumbent gives only a procedure for the circle, so rollouts re-derived the midpoint/half-distance from scratch or ran a full x+iy completion of the square as well; the revision splits the modulus into two explicit steps and supplies closed-form center and radius so the circle step is a substitution.

hints.hint: Union = areas summed minus overlap, so minimize overlap. Put the shared point at the origin and settle membership by signed half-plane tests. A corner placed at an interior point of shape S covers a wedge there, so the overlap is positive and strictly less than S: reject any claim that they touch in one point or that one lies wholly inside the other. Prove invariance rather than sampling angles. If that point is a k-fold rotational-symmetry center of S and the wedge angle is exactly 2*pi/k with both edges exiting S, rotation by 2*pi/k maps S to itself and sends the wedge to the next one, so the k wedge positions cut S into k equal pieces. Overlap is then area(S)/k at every rotation, so minimum equals maximum: compute that one area, report the union, stop. Build a piecewise area function and test its breakpoints only if the wedge angle differs from 2*pi/k.
hints.subagent_summary: Round-5 training with the incumbent fell to 4/8, and all four failures share one root cause: the invariance check is run as two independently guessed sample orientations, so a botched rotated-case value (one rollout got a single-point overlap and answered 5, another got a whole-shape overlap, a third got a value disagreeing with the aligned case) either ends the rollout wrong or triggers an open-ended piecewise search that ran out the 16384-token budget in three of eight. Winners instead trusted the aligned computation and argued invariance directly. This revision replaces sample-and-compare with an explicit one-line rotation-symmetry proof (rotating by 2*pi/k maps S to itself and permutes the k wedge positions, partitioning S into k equal pieces) plus a hard floor rejecting single-point and full-containment overlaps, so the student never needs a second computed orientation to commit.

hints.hint: When each term of a required pattern may come from any of N given functions, comparing adjacent terms proves nothing: neighbours can use different functions. Write the pattern's value at index n as T(n), then partition used indices by which function produced them. On P's group the only condition is P(n) = T(n), so those indices are roots of P - T, not identically zero since low-degree T cannot cancel P's leading term. So one function serves at most deg P indices: the root count deg P, not the interpolation count deg P + 1. That cap is per function, never the final count; each of the N functions gets its own group, so total = N x deg P. Reject any answer equal to deg P alone (bounds one group only) or to N alone (assumes one index per function). Confirm tightness by giving each function one block of consecutive indices and interpolating T there, then report the product.
hints.subagent_summary: My 8 public rollouts scored 5/8 and, unlike earlier rounds, all three failures terminated normally with wrong answers rather than truncating. Two derived a correct per-function root bound but then reported that cap as the final count instead of summing over the N functions, and one of those used the interpolation count deg P + 1 rather than the root count deg P; the third never used the root bound and assumed each function contributes exactly one index. The revision therefore fixes the cap to the root count and adds an explicit aggregation step plus reject-rules for the two observed off-by-a-factor endings.

hints.hint: Fit the parameters first: log_c u = y means u = c^y, so each given point gives one linear equation. A single vector equality only says parallelogram, so carry one unknown: write a vertex as (t, f(t)), translate by the given displacement, and require the image to lie on the curve too. A midpoint or vertex-sum condition restates that and over-determines t. Subtracting the two log equations turns the y-gap into one multiplicative factor on the argument, leaving a rational equation. Reject roots repeating a given vertex or making an argument nonpositive, then get each new vertex y by substituting back into f, since base under 1 flips signs. Area = shoelace.
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 public rollouts were correct (train_i=1.0), so train is saturated and only transfer binds; heldout has tracked hint length inversely across rounds (73 tok -> 0.15, 151 -> 0.1375, 161 -> 0.125, 189 -> 0.075), so this revision is shorter than the 151-token incumbent. The three longest correct rollouts thrashed on hundreds of midpoint/vertex-sum lines and contradiction talk after adding a redundant second closure condition, while the short clean rollouts carried one on-curve parameter; historical failures on this hint instead assigned the translated vertex a y from the carried shift rather than from f, got a point off the graph, and reported an area anyway. The hint keeps only the portable pipeline plus those two cheap guards and drops the narrow discriminant-flip and exponential-form verbosity.

hints.hint: The middle pile is a stack, so a whole final order is produced by exactly one legal push/pop word, no other route reaches it. Hence never count permutations, never assume the order is forced: write the word the asked event demands, then price it. Price a move 1/2 only where both a push and a pop are legal; the move is forced, factor 1, when the source is empty or nothing is left to push. Multiply factors along the word. If the event fixes only one position instead of the whole order, sum over the words that satisfy it. Fix orientation first: the bottom of a pile is whatever was placed on it earliest, the top whatever was placed last.
hints.subagent_summary: My 8 public rollouts scored 0/8 in two clusters: four asserted the delivery order is deterministically reversed, and three assumed uniformity (one answer per permutation, or per which item lands last); one exhausted its token budget on unstructured enumeration. Rounds 1-4 showed that longer enumerate-the-tree hints all cost held-out relative to the 83-token incumbent, so this revision stays short and swaps the abstract state-graph advice for one portable structural fact: an output order corresponds to a unique legal push/pop word, which simultaneously refutes the forced-outcome and equiprobable-permutation fallacies and reduces the task to pricing that word by its free-versus-forced moves.

hints.hint: Interpret the unknown coefficients as weights of a linear functional evaluated at distinct nodes: the vanishing conditions say it kills a whole range of monomials, and the last condition fixes its scale. Since no constant is prescribed, first factor one power of the node out of each weight so the killed exponents begin at degree 0; then the functional simply returns the top coefficient of any polynomial inside the allowed degree. To isolate one weight, feed it the monic polynomial vanishing at every other node, evaluate that product at your node rather than expanding it, and undo the factoring. If you test a small analogue, scale the number of conditions with the number of unknowns and keep the same exponent range; a mis-scaled toy looks inconsistent and will mislead you.
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 rollouts scored 0 (7 hit the 16384-token cap): every one reinterpreted the rows as a polynomial in the condition number rather than the node, producing a degree-2005 polynomial with only 2004 roots, then spent the budget resolving the phantom free root and reported 1/2005, 0, or a harmonic sum. Two rollouts built a small analogue but gave it more conditions than unknowns, so the toy came out inconsistent and they abandoned the correct framing. This revision keeps the incumbent's proven functional opening and adds the two missing mechanical steps: absorb one node power into each weight so the annihilated exponents start at degree 0 (which is why the functional reads off a top coefficient), and scale the toy's condition count with its unknown count.

hints.hint: When the count N of identical units is not given, never lift a number straight from the story: a stated number of equal groups counts groups, not units, so it only forces N to be a multiple of that number. Recover N from integrality instead: if each per-unit share must be whole, N divides every listed total, so N is a common divisor of them all and the intended value is the largest admissible one, their gcd. Divisibility is necessary but not sufficient, since every divisor of the gcd also passes, so do not stop at a small candidate that happens to divide everything; go to the maximum. Decide once whether each listed figure is a grand total or a per-unit amount, then stop revisiting it. Finally sum all components, divide by N, and apply any markup or discount as one multiplicative factor; scaling and dividing commute. Check that each per-unit value is whole and the units match the question.
hints.subagent_summary: 5/8 public rollouts were correct; all three failures shared one mode, and it was not arithmetic: they read the stated number of equal groups as the unit count, divided every listed total by it, saw each quotient come out whole, and treated that successful divisibility check as confirmation, so they never ran the gcd/maximum-admissible-count step at all. The incumbent already warns that group wording only imposes a multiple constraint, but it sits mid-paragraph after the gcd sentence and was missed. I front-loaded that warning and added the portable closing of the loophole, namely that divisibility is necessary but not sufficient because every divisor of the gcd also passes, so one must continue to the maximum.

hints.hint: If p(q(x))=q(p(x)) with p,q the same degree n, do not grind the degree-n^2 coefficient system - that is where attempts stall and run out of room. Instead look for a common fixed point r and try the jointly centered form p(x)=r+A(x-r)^n, q(x)=r+B(x-r)^n. Composing forces AB^n=BA^n; factor that once as AB(A^(n-1)-B^(n-1))=0 and carry both branches, since B=A collapses to p=q. Let the given data, not a guessed sign, kill a branch. On the sign-flipped branch the given values combine symmetrically: their sum cancels the (x-r)^n terms and pins r, their difference pins A. Verify p(r)=q(r)=r and check the identity at one spare point. Then evaluate only the requested inputs in centered form, never expanding.
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 public rollouts were correct again (8/8, 4.4k-6.0k tokens, none truncated), so the training question stays saturated and every remaining point is transfer; the one visible waste is that some rollouts burned ~3k tokens looping on the algebra of AB^n=BA^n (repeatedly mis-cancelling before recovering B=+-A) and others accepted B=-A purely on the hint's authority. Across rounds only the round-2 proposal raised heldout (0.175), and its distinctive ingredient was the factored condition AB(A^(n-1)-B^(n-1))=0 with an instruction to carry both branches and let data eliminate one, while its train loss came from abstracting the trigger and dropping the fixed-point/verify steps. This revision therefore keeps the incumbent's concrete p(q)=q(p) trigger, centered ansatz, and verification spine untouched and swaps only the asserted odd-n sign for that factored both-branch derivation, so unseen problems whose data favours the B=A branch are not forced into a sign flip.

hints.hint: One operation means ALL listed sub-steps in order, each applied to the state the previous sub-step produced; count repeats of the whole operation, never of one sub-step. Write states as distinct labels. Swap two adjacent length-B blocks by moving each as a rigid unit carrying its CURRENT contents: new prefix = (current slots B+1..2B)(current slots 1..B), tail unchanged. The fatal slip is refilling a block from the ORIGINAL letters, silently undoing an earlier sub-step; after each sub-step check every label appears once and that your line came from the previous line. Overlapping sub-steps give no involution: before answering 2, apply the operation twice and look. Then write the state after each full operation on its own line until it first matches the original. Do the two smallest sizes exactly, fit a closed form, confirm on one larger size, and commit. If a line looks wrong redo it, never restart.
hints.subagent_summary: Only 2/8 correct and six of six failures hit the token cap; all six produced a smallest-size count that contradicted their own larger-size count and then looped for thousands of tokens re-deriving it. Tracing the block swaps shows the shared root cause is refilling a swapped block from the original letters instead of the state the previous sub-step produced, which silently undoes an earlier sub-step and makes the operation look like an involution. The revision therefore states the rigid-unit rule with CURRENT contents, adds a came-from-the-previous-line check, and tells the student to commit once one larger size confirms the closed form instead of restarting.
